title: Hello, I'm Budi
goal: Greet people, introduce yourself, ask how someone is, and build your first Hebrew sentences — which turn out to need no "is" and no "a".
bekal: say hello and goodbye at the right time of day
say who you are and what you do
choose the right "you" for a man or a woman

dialogs.title: שִׂיחָה — בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה
dialogs.intro: Budi has just arrived in Tel Aviv. In a university corridor he runs into Noa.

lines.speaker: נֹעָה:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. I'm Noa.

lines.speaker: נֹעָה:
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. And you?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: I'm not a student. I'm a teacher.

lines.speaker: נֹעָה:
lines.id: Oh, great! A teacher of what?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: מוֹרֶה לְאַנְגְּלִית. אֲבָל עַכְשָׁו אֲנִי תַּלְמִיד.
lines.baca: moreh le'anglit. aval akhshav ani talmid.
lines.id: An English teacher. But right now I'm a learner.
lines.literal: teacher for-english. but now I pupil.

notes: **שָׁלוֹם** is the first word you'll learn and the one you'll hear most in Israel. It means "peace", and it's used for both **hello** and **goodbye** — just like *aloha*. When in doubt, שָׁלוֹם is never wrong.

⚠️ **מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ / מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ** — "how are you" changes according to **the person you're talking to**, not according to you. To a man: *mah shlomkha*. To a woman: *mah shlomekh*. In line 2 Budi is asking Noa, a woman, so he says *shlomekh*; asking David, he would say *mah shlomkha*. Literally it isn't "how are you" but **"what is your peace?"** — the same root as שָׁלוֹם.
**בְּסֵדֶר** (*beseder*) literally means "in order", and it's an all-purpose answer: fine, OK, sure, no problem. This word will save you hundreds of times.
**Notice what is NOT in the sentence אֲנִי בּוּדִי.** There is no "am". Hebrew just says "I Budi". In the present tense, Hebrew simply has no word for am/is/are — so stop looking for one.
**And something else is missing: "a".** אֲנִי מוֹרֶה = "I teacher". Hebrew has no equivalent of *a/an* at all.
⚠️ **לֹא** (*lo*) means both "no" **and** "not". אֲנִי לֹא סְטוּדֶנְט = "I'm not a student". It always comes **right before** the word it negates — no "do not", no "am not", just לֹא.

**Jobs have a masculine and a feminine form.** מוֹרֶה (teacher, m) → מוֹרָה (teacher, f); סְטוּדֶנְט → סְטוּדֶנְטִית. The most common patterns: add ־ָה or ־ִית. Calling yourself by the wrong form sounds like getting your own name wrong.
**נָעִים מְאֹד** (*na'im me'od*, "very pleasant") is "nice to meet you". It's the same for men and women — learn it as a single chunk.

⚠️ **The stress is almost always on the LAST syllable.** *sha-LOM*, *to-DAH*, *be-SE-der* (this one's an exception), *le-hit-ra-OT*. English speakers tend to stress earlier; if you say *SHA-lom*, Israelis will still understand, but it sounds like a brand name, not a greeting.

grammars.title: Sentences with no verb: the basic pattern
body: The most basic Hebrew sentence just puts two things side by side: **who** + **what/how they are**. There's nothing linking them.
after: Compare the English — *I am Budi*, *she is a student* — and you'll see how much work Hebrew skips. This pattern holds all the way to the last unit.

grammars.title: Four ways to say "you"
body: English gets by with one "you"; Hebrew has four, and it's better to set them up in unit 1 than to put it off. You choose by **who you're talking to**.

head: To
Hebrew
Say it
Example
rows: אַתָּה מוֹרֶה? — are you a teacher?
אַתְּ מוֹרָה? — are you a teacher?
אַתֶּם תַּלְמִידִים? — are you all learners?
אַתֶּן מוֹרוֹת? — are you all teachers?

after: ⚠️ Look at אַתָּה and אַתְּ: **both are spelled את**; only the niqqud tells them apart. Once you read Hebrew without niqqud, you'll have to guess from context — one reason Israelis often say the pronoun in full.

Modern Hebrew has **no polite "you"** (like French *vous*). To a minister, a professor, or a grandfather, Israelis still say אַתָּה. Politeness comes through tone and words like בְּבַקָּשָׁה, not through pronouns.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **לַיְלָה טוֹב is not a greeting.** It's only used for **parting** at night, like "sleep well". To greet someone in the evening, use עֶרֶב טוֹב.

blocks.title: Answering "how are you"
items: **בְּסֵדֶר** *(beseder)* — fine, OK. The safest and most common answer.
**וְאַתָּה? / וְאַתְּ?** *(ve'atah? / ve'at?)* — and you? Don't forget to ask back; in Israel, not asking back sounds cold.

sections.title: Naming jobs: two forms for one word

blocks.text: Three patterns cover almost every case: add **־ָה** (מוֹרֶה → מוֹרָה), add **־ִית** (סְטוּדֶנְט → סְטוּדֶנְטִית), or insert **־ֶ־ֶת** (מְהַנְדֵּס → מְהַנְדֶּסֶת). That third pattern is exactly the verb pattern you'll meet in unit 7 — not a coincidence.

please; here you go; you're welcome

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with אַתָּה or אַתְּ.
Put the words in the right order.
Write the feminine form of each job.

answers: אֲנִי מוֹרֶה — הִיא סְטוּדֶנְטִית — אֲנִי לֹא רוֹפֵא — בֹּקֶר טוֹב! — תּוֹדָה, לְהִתְרָאוֹת
אֲנִי לֹא מוֹרֶה — כֵּן, הִיא סְטוּדֶנְטִית — שָׁלוֹם, אֲנִי בּוּדִי — עַכְשָׁו אֲנַחְנוּ תַּלְמִידִים
wave: Before bed, say five sentences about yourself out loud using the pattern "אֲנִי ..." — your name, your job, and three things you are not (אֲנִי לֹא ...). Watch the stress on the last syllable.
